items.title: Longineu Parsons interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 17, 2026
items.q: thinking about people like Oliver Lake and the people I played with, well especially Cecil Taylor and Sun Ra.

ctx.x: The raw emotion and the freedom of it. He was free to express what he was feeling. He didn’t allow any of the so-called “rules” to get in the way. See when we are studying music, like as an academic I can tell you there’s rules this and rules that. And that’s B.S. There’s no such thing as a rule. These are performance practices. And then people came along and said this is the rule because if you’re doing Baroque music and Baroque counterpoint this is how J.S. Bach did it. Basically what they’re saying, “Therefore…

American song form from some show or whatever, okay, great song, great pieces of work. As a classical composer it’s not all that exciting to me. So I’m looking at how I can bring all of this together. And thinking about people like Henry Threadgill and thinking about people like Oliver Lake and the people I played with, well especially Cecil Taylor and Sun Ra. They’re looking for ways to do things, for new ways. Or finding ways to just express who they are. And why should that expression be restricted to what…

If you have a student trumpet player working on improvisation and they constantly are playing – well let’s say an F sharp over a B flat chord. Is there a difference between playing outside the chord if you do it on purpose or if you’re not aware that you’re doing it?
